title: Exposure to fake news on social media, coping mechanisms, and mental health impact among Vietnamese adolescents and young adults
screen_reason: Online cross-sectional survey of 1,850 Vietnamese adolescents and young adults (September to October 2021). Reports a self-reported exposure share with a denominator (68.8% encountered fake news on social networking sites at least occasionally) and a self-reported sharing share (7.1% joined in to share fake news at least occasionally). Both are RECALL estimates.

estimates.country: Vietnam (Hanoi, Tuyen Quang and Can Tho)
estimates.platform: Social networking sites (SNS), not broken out by platform; the paper notes Vietnamese youth use mainly Facebook, Zalo and YouTube
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who report encountering fake news on social networking sites occasionally, regularly or always
estimates.denominator: 1,850 Vietnamese adolescents and young adults recruited by online snowball sampling in three cities (mean age 17.0, 92.9% students, 91.5% urban, 57.0% female)
estimates.definition: Answered occasionally, regularly or always to the 5-point item 'Have you ever encountered fake news on SNS? If yes, how is the frequency?' (1 = Never to 5 = Always); never/rarely counted as no
estimates.misinfo_def: Fake news is defined as 'fake stories that might appear to be news, spread on the Internet or other media', and such fabricated content often resembles actual news, making it difficult for audiences to distinguish between truth and falsehood
estimates.source_quote: Among 1850 participants, the majority of them (68.8%) reported at least occasionally encountering fake news on SNS.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 2; Table 1 total row (Never/rarely 577, 31.2; Occasionally/regularly/always 1273, 68.8; Total 1850)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent's own judgement on a single 5-point frequency item; no definition of fake news was supplied to respondents in the reported instrument and no external verification was performed
estimates.moderator_quote: Out of a total of 1929 individuals invited to participate in the study, a 95.9% completion rate was achieved, with 1850 respondents completing the questionnaire. Sampling and recruitment This study employed the snowball sampling methodology in a four-step procedure, as follows:
estimates.notes: Threshold is 'occasionally or more' on a 5-point Never-to-Always scale; the paper never reports the five response levels separately, so no stricter (regularly/always) variant can be extracted. Sample is not population-representative: online snowball recruitment starting from student union presidents, 92.9% students, 91.5% urban, mean age 17.0. sampling_frame coded convenience for the snowball design. The paper compares its figure with a Pew estimate of 72% for Vietnam; that is a cited external number and is not extracted.

estimates.country: Vietnam (Hanoi, Tuyen Quang and Can Tho)
estimates.platform: Social networking sites (SNS), not broken out by platform
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who report joining in to share fake news occasionally, regularly or always
estimates.denominator: 1,850 Vietnamese adolescents and young adults recruited by online snowball sampling in three cities
estimates.definition: Scored occasionally, regularly or always on the two-item 'join in to share the fake news' coping domain (5-point scale, 1 = Never to 5 = Always), described as engagement with fake news where participants contribute to its spread; never/rarely counted as no
estimates.misinfo_def: Fake news is defined as 'fake stories that might appear to be news, spread on the Internet or other media', and such fabricated content often resembles actual news, making it difficult for audiences to distinguish between truth and falsehood
estimates.source_quote: Nearly half tended to ignore fake news (47.1%), while fewer intervened to counter its spread (16.2%) or joined in sharing it (7.1%).
estimates.page_loc: Abstract; Results p. 2; Table 2, 'Join-in to share the fake news', Occasionally/regularly/always: 131, 7.1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent's own judgement on a two-item Likert coping domain (Cronbach's alpha 0.81 reported for the nine-item coping question as a whole); no external verification of any shared item
estimates.moderator_quote: coping strategies when encountering fake news were assessed using nine items, grouped into three domains: (1) ignore the fake news (this domain encompasses efforts to counter fake news and prevent its spread), (2) intervene to prevent the spread of the fake news (This domain encompasses efforts to counter fake news and prevent its spread), and (3) join in to share the fake news (This domain refers to engagement with fake news, where participants contribute to its spread).
estimates.notes: The item wording of the two 'join in to share' items is only shown in Figure 1, which is not readable in this text, so the exact numerator wording cannot be verified beyond the domain description. The Methods contain a copy-paste error: domain (1) 'ignore the fake news' is given the description belonging to domain (2) ('encompasses efforts to counter fake news and prevent its spread'), which does not affect this row but does undermine confidence in the instrument description. The share is conditional on the whole sample, not on those exposed. Sentence in Results reads 'or report to share it (7.1%)', evidently a typo for 'joined in to share'; the Abstract wording is used as the source quote.

missed_or_uncertain: Considered and not extracted: (1) coping shares that are not misinformation exposure or sharing — ignoring fake news at least occasionally (47.1%, 871/1850) and intervening to prevent its spread (16.2%, 300/1850); these describe reactions to fake news, not the amount of misinformation encountered or spread. (2) Figure 1 coping percentages quoted in the text (32.3% occasionally and 27.9% always ignore; 'more than 80%' would find the correct information but do nothing else; 56.4% would not find similar news to read/share) — same reason, and the first two are sub-levels of the 47.1% row rather than distinct estimates. (3) Figure 2 recognition percentages (42.8% and 11.5% perceived news reliable or very reliable with a professionally certified poster; 40.9% and 9.1% if the source was stated; 19.7% and 7.1% unreliable/totally unreliable for sharing by others) — perceived-credibility cue ratings, not shares of misinformation, and the sentence describing them is internally garbled. (4) Scale means with no share (Ignore 6.4, Intervene 11.6, Join-in 3.6, PHQ-9 7.4, GAD-7 4.9, BSMAS 8.1, literacy and recognition domain scores). (5) Externally cited figures in the Introduction and Discussion (Pew: over 80% concerned about made-up news across 35 countries; ~70% of SNS users in 11 emerging economies; Vietnam 72%, Tunisia 78%, Lebanon 75%, Jordan 71%; 'false news spreads six times faster'; '70% of users struggle to distinguish truth from falsehood') — all cited from elsewhere, excluded by R8. (6) Sample composition figures (92.9% students, 91.5% urban, 57.0% female, SNS-use durations) and the 95.9% completion rate.

rob.design: Online cross-sectional survey, SurveyMonkey, September to October 2021, in Hanoi, Tuyen Quang and Can Tho. Non-probability four-step snowball recruitment starting from student union presidents, who forwarded the link through their networks; 1,929 invited, 1,850 analysed after listwise deletion of 79 incomplete cases (95.9% completion). No response rate in the usual sense is calculable for a snowball chain. The exposure measure is a single 5-point self-report item; coping is a nine-item Likert instrument (alpha 0.81); digital literacy (alpha 0.91/0.92), recognition (0.85/0.87), BSMAS (0.97), PHQ-9 (0.92), GAD-7 (0.94). Instrument developed from a literature review, refined by an expert panel, back-translated for the standard scales, and piloted on 20 students. No external coding of content, so no coder reliability applies. Authors acknowledge selection bias, cross-sectional design and self-report/recall bias as limitations.
rob.item6_quote: We used a 5-point Likert question "Have you ever encountered fake news on SNS? If yes, how is the frequency?" to measure participant's experiences and encounters with fake news. The question was scored from 1 "Never" to 5 "Always".
rob.item10_quote: Among 1850 participants, the majority of them (68.8%) reported at least occasionally encountering fake news on SNS.
